extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, assessing, and applying inductive generalizations (both universal and approximate), including how to weigh evidence, combine probabilistic premises, and when to treat approximations as conditional universals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical-law limitation of observed uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of co-existence (including those that appear ultimate or arise from laws of causes yet undetected) are entitled to reception only as empirical laws and are not to be presumed true except within the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which the observations were made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizations based on enumeration must be held only within the scope of actual observation and adjacent cases; new counter-instances discovered outside those limits can legitimately overturn the generalization. Examples: the 'all crows are black' generalization is only empirical within observed limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish properties as causal effects vs properties of Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property varies among individuals of the same Kind, it is likely an effect of causation; if it never varies in observed instances, it may be a property of Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When variation is observed (e.g., flower colors), treat the property as derivative and seek causal explanations; when constant among simple substances, treat as ultimate only with caution. This affects whether a generalization indicates a common cause or a true Kind-difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine all subordinate species before generalizing across superior Kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal propositions respecting properties of superior Kinds, unless grounded on proved or presumed connection by causation, ought not to be hazarded except after separately examining every known sub-kind (infimæ species) included in the larger Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer 'true of all animals' from seeing the property in some animals unless either a causal connection is known or every sub-kind has been checked; historical attempts to generalize among simple substances failed when sub-kinds were not fully examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger evidence required for more general claims
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires much more evidence to establish an exception to one of the more general empirical laws than to the more special ones; the degree of incredulity increases with the generality of the experience contradicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reported white crow in a well-explored locality is more credible than a claim that contradicts universal properties of animals or matter; weigh novelty against the scope of the generalization it would overturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations evaluated by proportion of confirming instances
rubrics_metrics.description: A probable inference based on an approximate generalization of form 'Most A are B' has degree of probability depending on the proportion of instances which accord with the generalization versus those that conflict with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible quantify frequency (e.g., nine of ten) to estimate error chances; such propositions are valuable as steps toward universal truths and as practical guides when universals are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two contexts for relying on 'Most A are B' (only data vs known causes/marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate generalizations may either be the whole of our knowledge (we only know 'Most A are B') or a practical shorthand when we know the causes or distinguishing marks but cannot investigate each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If causes/marks are known, use indirect checks (e.g., frequency of cause) to support the approximation; if not, rely on varied enumeration but limit conclusions to observed circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of approximate generalizations limited to empirical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Most A are B' propositions, when admissible, are admissible only as empirical laws and only within the limits of place, time, and circumstance under which they have been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extrapolating approximate generalizations to different cultural or circumstantial domains (example: trusting an approximate claim about judges across societies without local evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer checking specific causes/marks over applying coarse averages
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, replace uncertain average-based indications by checking for the existence of the cause or mark in the particular case (direct recognition of cause is superior to applying 'Most' generalizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: rather than relying only on 'most people tell the truth', examine witness-specific marks (honesty, accuracy, interest) which may be approximated themselves but allow a firmer judgment for the individual case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use general averages only for cases known to be average
rubrics_metrics.description: A general average (e.g., nine out of ten) should be applied only to cases which are neither known nor can be presumed to be other than average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Averages inform decisions about large numbers (insurance tables) but poorly predict individual cases or known sub-classes; adjust with additional information about the particular instance if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine approximate generalizations by addition (independent) or deduction (chaining)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying two or more approximate generalizations to the same case, they may cooperate by addition (each directly applicable, raising overall probability) or by deduction/ratiocination (one applies only via the other, which reduces resultant probability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addition example: two independent witnesses. Deduction example: hearsay-of-hearsay. Use probability calculations when independence can be assumed; expect diminished probability in chained deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require independence when multiplying probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability computations joining approximate generalizations assume the probabilities arising from different classes are independent; if A and C are connected, multiplication logic fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not independent, overlaps may make the combined probability equal to the single premise; check whether not-Bs in one class are identical with not-Bs in the other before combining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error accumulates multiplicatively in sequential approximate reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When approximate generalizations are chained (Most A are B; Most B are C; etc.), the probability of the terminal conclusion diminishes multiplicatively at each step and can quickly become negligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical example: 9/10 × 8/9 × 7/8 = 7/10; a few chained steps can erode confidence substantially—hence limit the length of such chains or increase premises' proximity to universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two exceptional cases where approximates can be treated like universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate generalizations may be carried as far as universal laws if they can be transformed into exact universal propositions by annexing explicit provisos/conditions that capture the known distinguishing factors of exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can state a proviso (e.g., 'All persons with uncontrolled power employ it ill, provided they are not persons of unusual judgment and rectitude'), then reason as with universals but carry forward the hypothesis/conditions to track how far conclusions are applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical decision-making: corroborate imperfect indications
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical emergencies where decisive action is needed, use multiple indications which, though individually fallible, corroborate one another rather than awaiting perfectly conclusive evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid indecisiveness characteristic of some scientific minds in emergencies; aim to obtain corroborating indications to offset the incompleteness of any single approximate generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs indirect modes of ascertaining frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether 'Most A are B' holds, use either direct observation of the effect (frequency of B among A) or indirect inquiry into the frequency of the causes/marks of B (e.g., education as cause of literacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the mode that is more accessible or reliable in the context; often both modes will be combined to strengthen the induction.
